extracted.intended_audience: Speculative-fiction writers (fantasy/sci‑fi) who want guidance on writing characters outside their own background
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and practical criteria for portraying characters who differ from the author (different race, gender, sexuality, age, disability, culture) with authenticity and care, especially for writers of fantasy and science fiction. Emphasizes terminology, research, exercises, and avoiding common anti‑patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write what you don't know — but do it right
rubrics_metrics.description: “Simple. You write what you don’t know…but you do it right (or exert every effort to do so).”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book's central exhortation: authors may and should attempt to write characters outside their experience, but must make every effort to do it correctly — which implies research, attention, humility, and concrete practice. The reviewer emphasizes this as the core lesson and framing of the book.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research is required
rubrics_metrics.description: “Invariably, research is involved,” as pointed out in Shawl’s essay 'Beautiful Strangers.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should undertake substantive research into cultures, histories, experiences, and contexts different from their own rather than relying on intuition or stereotypes. Research is presented as necessary to authenticity and to avoiding offensive mistakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize and avoid the Unmarked State
rubrics_metrics.description: Unmarked State: the default setting of a character not otherwise described — usually white, male, single, young, heterosexual, and without disability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers must be conscious when their characters occupy the ‘default’ unmarked position and understand how that framing centers privilege; explicitly marking difference or acknowledging the unmarked default can prevent erasure and invisibility of other identities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Glory Syndrome
rubrics_metrics.description: Glory Syndrome: the story is about the problems of those marked by difference, but only insofar as they affect those who are unmarked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not center the narrative value of marginalized characters solely in how their experience validates or enlightens unmarked characters. Ensure marked characters have agency and fully realized perspectives rather than serving as props for unmarked protagonists' growth or triumph.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use parallax — adopt character‑centered norms
rubrics_metrics.description: Parallax involves being conscious of what a character with a particular history/context would consider to be 'normal.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write from the internal logic and assumptions of the character's lived experience rather than imposing the author's or the dominant culture’s notion of normal. This means recalibrating sensory details, values, and expected behaviors to the character’s frame.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use resonance to reinforce cultural/contextual detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Resonance: a complex of ideas that reinforce and highlight one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create clusters of consistent details, symbols, and thematic elements that mutually reinforce a character’s cultural or contextual identity, which helps achieve depth and authenticity rather than isolated or tokenistic markers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid common missteps — follow the 'Don't Do This!' guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: The book includes a 'Don’t Do This!' section that goes through missteps some writers make and gives specific examples and counter‑examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for anti‑patterns such as generic exoticization or flattening (example given: 'the Dark Hordes attacked…'). The method is to present concrete bad examples and corrected versions so writers can see problematic assumptions and how to fix them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be rigorous in questioning your assumptions and presuppositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers must be aware of marked states and positions of privilege and be rigorous in questioning their own assumptions and presuppositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self‑interrogation is a required practice: examine why you make certain narrative choices, whose perspective you center, and which details you omit. The book encourages sustained critical reflection as part of the writing process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim for authenticity and believability
rubrics_metrics.description: The goal is that it is possible to write characters of a different race, gender, or sexual orientation in a way that is authentic and believable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive to create characters whose identities feel lived‑in and plausible rather than caricatured. Authenticity is achieved through research, perspective-taking, consistent detail (resonance), and avoiding flattening tropes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept imperfection but continue striving
rubrics_metrics.description: The authors acknowledge it's likely writers will still get something wrong even after reading the book, but that’s okay; the goal is worth striving for.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Embrace humility and iterative improvement: mistakes are possible and learning continues. The standard is not perfection but conscientious effort, responsiveness to critique, and ongoing work to do better.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincere and appropriate cultural appropriation
rubrics_metrics.description: Shawl's essay 'Beautiful Strangers: Transracial Writing for the Sincere and Appropriate Cultural Appropriation' addresses when and how appropriation can be approached.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If writing across cultures, aim for sincerity and appropriateness: be mindful of power dynamics, avoid exploitative or extractive portrayals, and take steps (research, consultation, sensitivity) to reduce harm. The book treats appropriate appropriation as possible but demanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach through exercises and concrete, practical advice
rubrics_metrics.description: Each main section pairs an extended essay with writing exercises — a holdover from the workshops — reflecting the book’s subtitle, A Practical Approach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learning is meant to be active: apply lessons through targeted exercises to practice perspective-taking and to test revised approaches. The reviewer highlights the exercises as a reason the book is useful as a textbook for writers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use terminology to make invisible problems visible
rubrics_metrics.description: Introducing terms (Unmarked State, Glory Syndrome, parallax, resonance) causes perspective shifts and makes issues in a text visible that an author might otherwise miss.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn and apply precise vocabulary to diagnose and discuss representational problems; naming patterns helps authors spot and correct issues in their own work and in peers’ work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ specific examples and counter‑examples as a revision tool
rubrics_metrics.description: The authors provide concrete examples and counter‑examples to reveal problematic assumptions and omissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use side‑by‑side bad/good examples during revision to identify exactly what makes a line or scene problematic and what a better alternative looks like; this is presented as a practical technique for rewriting and improving scenes.
